warmup.q: Three cook threads take orders from a BlockingQueue, a queue whose take() waits while it's empty. At closing time, the head chef puts ONE special "kitchen closed" item in the queue, and each cook stops when it takes that item. What happens?
options: All three cooks stop, because they all see the item
One cook stops; the other two wait in take() forever
The queue throws, because the item can only be taken once
Nothing stops until the queue is garbage collected
warmup.why: The special item, a poison pill, is just an element: the first cook to take it removes it from the queue and stops. The other two find an empty queue and wait in take() forever, and anything that waits for them, such as the program's shutdown, hangs too. You need one pill per cook. The first section runs exactly this.

opening:
Picture the kitchen from wait, notify and guarded blocks at closing time. The waiters have stopped taking orders. A few tickets are still on the rail, and three cooks are working through them. (In code, each cook is a thread, one path of work running beside the others, and the rail is a queue.) When the rail is empty, each cook waits for the next ticket. Tonight there won't be one.

How does a cook know it's time to go home? An empty rail can mean the evening is over, or just that the next ticket is late. The quickest answers both go wrong. Tell every cook to stop at once, and the tickets still on the rail are never cooked. Put one "kitchen closed" card on the rail, and one cook goes home while two wait by the empty rail all night.

Don't share ended with the state you can't take away. This lesson puts the whole track's tools to work on three classic problems: closing the kitchen, five philosophers sharing forks at a round table, and a price board that many read and one person changes. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at closing time, with three cooks by an empty rail who couldn't tell the evening was over. One pill per cook sent them home after the last order. Then we unfroze a table of philosophers with one fork order, and let the owner change prices without waiting for the shop to empty.

Now search your own code for loops around take(), and ask how each one ends. If it's an interrupt, check what happens to the work still queued. If it's a pill, count the pills.

Every fix here passed its demo. Next, we'll ask how you know a fix really works: how do you write a test that makes threads collide, and what do you do when a program hangs anyway?

sections.h: Closing the kitchen: a bounded queue and one poison pill per cook
sections.html:
Let's name the parts first. A thread that puts work into a queue is a producer, and a thread that takes work out is a consumer. Our waiters are producers and our cooks are consumers, and the whole shape is called producer-consumer. Most concurrent programs have one somewhere: something makes work at one speed, and something else does it at another.

In Java, the rail is a BlockingQueue from Concurrent collections. put adds a ticket, and take removes one, waiting while the queue is empty. Give the queue a limit, as the rail in wait, notify and guarded blocks had. A bounded queue, one with a fixed capacity, makes put wait while it's full, so a fast waiter slows to the cooks' pace instead of piling up tickets until memory runs out. That's backpressure: a full queue pushing back on whoever fills it.

The hard part is stopping. A cook waits in take(), and take() never returns from an empty queue. Inside, it parks (sleeps until woken) on the queue's own "not empty" condition, a wait set like the one from guarded blocks, and only a put wakes it. Once the waiters have gone home, nothing ever will.

There are three ways out. Interrupting the cooks, that is, asking each thread to stop, is fast. But it drops whatever is still queued: take() checks the interrupt flag before it looks at the queue, so it throws even when tickets are waiting. Polling with a timeout, poll(1, SECONDS) in a loop that checks a stop flag, works too. But every cook can wait up to one timeout before it notices, and every loop has to check the flag correctly. The clean answer is a poison pill: a special item that means "no more work", put on the rail like any other ticket. A cook that takes it stops.

Here's the naive version, with one pill for the whole kitchen:

Java
// Naive: one pill for three cooks
for (Thread w : waiters) w.join();      // every order is on the rail
rail.put(PILL);                          // "kitchen closed"
for (Thread c : cooks) c.join();         // waits for all three cooks
Kotlin
// Naive: one pill for three cooks
waiters.forEach { it.join() }           // every order is on the rail
rail.put(PILL)                           // "kitchen closed"
cooks.forEach { it.join() }              // waits for all three cooks

The Try it runs two waiters, three cooks and a rail with room for four tickets. With -Pargs=onepill it printed:

cook-1 got its pill after 1004 orders
cooks still waiting: 2 (WAITING in take)

A pill is just an item, so the first cook to take it removes it from the rail and goes home. The other two find an empty rail and wait in take(), all night. Anything that waits for them to finish, such as the program's own shutdown, hangs with them.

Three rules make pills work:

  • Put the pills only after every producer has finished, so they land behind every real ticket.
  • Put one pill per consumer, because each pill is taken once.
  • Compare against the pill by identity, with ==. A pill made with new String("PILL") is an object of its own, so a real ticket that happens to read PILL is still a ticket.
Java
// each cook
while (true) {
    String ticket = rail.take();          // waits while the rail is empty
    if (ticket == PILL) break;            // identity: a ticket that reads "PILL" is still a ticket
    cook(ticket);
}

// the head chef, after every waiter has finished:
for (int i = 0; i < cooks; i++) rail.put(PILL);   // one pill per cook
Kotlin
// each cook
while (true) {
    val ticket = rail.take()              // waits while the rail is empty
    if (ticket === PILL) break            // identity: a ticket that reads "PILL" is still a ticket
    cook(ticket)
}

// the head chef, after every waiter has finished:
repeat(cooks) { rail.put(PILL) }          // one pill per cook

The same run with one pill per cook printed:

cook-1 got its pill after 511 orders
cook-2 got its pill after 177 orders
cook-0 got its pill after 1312 orders
cooks still waiting: 0

The three counts add up to 2,000, every order the waiters put, and no cook was left waiting. The split changes from run to run, because whichever cook is free takes the next ticket. The figure shows the rail at closing time: the last real orders, then the pills.

One pill stops one consumer. Put one per consumer, after the last producer.

The kitchen now closes without losing an order. The next problem has no queue at all, just five threads, five locks and a table.

try.title: One pill per cook, or not
steps: Read PoisonPills. Two waiters put 1,000 orders each on a rail with room for 4, and three cooks take them. After the waiters finish, main puts the pills.
Run it. Note how many orders each cook handled.
Run it with -Pargs=onepill. Predict how many cooks are still waiting after one second, and in which thread state.

code.title: PoisonPills.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; /** * Closing time in the kitchen: two waiters (producers), three cooks (consumers), one bounded rail, * shut down with poison pills. Run with -Pargs=onepill to send a single pill instead of one per cook. */ public class PoisonPills { @SuppressWarnings("StringOperationCanBeSimplified") static final String PILL = new String("PILL"); // compared by identity public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { boolean onePill = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("onepill"); BlockingQueue<String> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4); List<Thread> cooks = new ArrayList<>(); for (int c = 0; c < 3; c++) { Thread t = new Thread(() -> { int done = 0; try { while (true) { String r = queue.take(); if (r == PILL) break; // this cook stops; the others keep going done++; } System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " got its pill after " + done + " orders"); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "cook-" + c); t.setDaemon(true); t.start(); cooks.add(t); } Thread[] waiters = new Thread[2]; for (int p = 0; p < 2; p++) { int me = p; waiters[p] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) queue.put("order-" + me + "-" + i); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "waiter-" + p); waiters[p].start(); } for (Thread t : waiters) t.join(); // 1. every waiter is done... for (int c = 0; c < (onePill ? 1 : cooks.size()); c++) queue.put(PILL); // 2. ...then one pill each for (Thread t : cooks) t.join(1_000); List<Thread> stuck = cooks.stream().filter(Thread::isAlive).toList(); System.out.println("cooks still waiting: " + stuck.size() + (stuck.isEmpty() ? "" : " (" + stuck.get(0).getState() + " in take)")); } }

alt.title: PoisonPills.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Closing time in the kitchen: two waiters (producers), three cooks (consumers), one bounded rail, // shut down with poison pills. Run with -Pargs=onepill to send a single pill instead of one per cook. private val PILL = String(charArrayOf('P', 'I', 'L', 'L')) // a fresh object: compared by identity fun main(args: Array<String>) { val onePill = args.firstOrNull() == "onepill" val queue = ArrayBlockingQueue<String>(4) val cooks = List(3) { c -> thread(isDaemon = true, name = "cook-$c") { var done = 0 while (true) { val r = queue.take() if (r === PILL) break // this cook stops; the others keep going done++ } println("${Thread.currentThread().name} got its pill after $done orders") } } val waiters = List(2) { me -> thread(name = "waiter-$me") { repeat(1_000) { i -> queue.put("order-$me-$i") } } } waiters.forEach { it.join() } // 1. every waiter is done... repeat(if (onePill) 1 else cooks.size) { queue.put(PILL) } // 2. ...then one pill each cooks.forEach { it.join(1_000) } val stuck = cooks.count { it.isAlive } println("cooks still waiting: $stuck" + if (stuck > 0) " (${cooks.last { it.isAlive }.state} in take)" else "") }

try.expect: With one pill each, all three cooks report their pill, their counts add up to 2,000, and cooks still waiting: 0. The split changes from run to run. With onepill, one cook stops and two are still waiting: cooks still waiting: 2 (WAITING in take). In a real program, that's a shutdown that never finishes.

aside.title: Why are these three called classic?
aside.html: Because people have argued about them for over fifty years. Edsger Dijkstra set the dining philosophers as an exam problem in 1965, with five computers competing for shared tape drives, and Tony Hoare soon retold it with philosophers and forks. The readers-writers problem got its name in a 1971 paper by Courtois, Heymans and Parnas. They have lasted because nearly every concurrency bug you'll meet is one of the three in another setting. It's a queue that won't stop, locks taken in a circle, or a thread that never gets its turn.

video.title: Closing the kitchen: a bounded rail makes the fast waiter wait, an empty rail can mean late, and one poison pill per cook, after the last waiter, sends every cook home

sections.h: Five philosophers, five forks: the table that freezes, and two fixes
sections.html:
Here's the most famous puzzle in concurrency, and it needs only a table. Five philosophers sit around a round table, with one fork between each pair of neighbours, so five forks in all. A philosopher thinks for a while, then gets hungry. To eat, each one needs both forks next to them, the one on the left and the one on the right, and each picks up the left fork first.

In code, each philosopher is a thread and each fork is a lock, a ReentrantLock from Explicit locks: an object a thread takes with lock() and gives back with unlock(). It works most of the time. Then, one day, all five get hungry at the same moment and each picks up a left fork. Let's trace the smallest version, with three philosophers:

  1. Philosopher 0 takes fork 0. At the same moment, philosopher 1 takes fork 1 and philosopher 2 takes fork 2.
  2. Philosopher 0 reaches for fork 1, which philosopher 1 holds. Philosopher 1 reaches for fork 2, held by philosopher 2.
  3. Philosopher 2 reaches for fork 0, held by philosopher 0. Every fork is in a hand, and nobody can eat.

Nobody puts a fork down, because the code never says to. That's the deadlock from Deadlock, livelock and starvation, threads that wait for each other forever, with three locks instead of two. All four of its conditions hold. Each fork has one owner (mutual exclusion). Each philosopher holds one fork while waiting for another (hold and wait). Nobody takes a fork from a neighbour (no preemption). And the waiting goes all the way round the table (circular wait). It's also what the bank's transfers look like when each one locks two of many accounts.

The simulator below has three philosophers. First let them eat one at a time. Then reset it and give each philosopher a single step before anyone takes a second.

The Try it runs five philosophers, 200 meals each, with a 1 ms pause between the two forks to make the bad moment likely. Left fork first, it printed:

naive: 0 of 1,000 meals in 3045 ms, deadlocked philosophers: 5

Zero meals, and the JVM itself, the program that runs your Java code, names all five philosophers as deadlocked, because forks that are ReentrantLocks have owners its deadlock detector can follow. There are two standard fixes, and each removes a different condition.

Resource ordering removes the circular wait. Number the forks and always take the lower-numbered one first. Philosophers 0 to 3 still take left, then right. Philosopher 4 needs forks 4 and 0, so it takes fork 0 first:

Java
int left = seat, right = (seat + 1) % forks.length;
ReentrantLock first = forks[Math.min(left, right)];    // philosopher 4 takes fork 0 first
ReentrantLock second = forks[Math.max(left, right)];
Kotlin
val left = seat
val right = (seat + 1) % forks.size
val first = forks[minOf(left, right)]     // philosopher 4 takes fork 0 first
val second = forks[maxOf(left, right)]

Now a philosopher who holds a fork and waits always wants a higher-numbered one. A cycle would need someone, somewhere, to wait for a lower number than the one they hold, so the cycle can't close, however many forks or accounts there are. It's the lock order from the bank's transfers, applied to a table.

A waiter removes the moment when everyone holds one fork. Only four of the five may sit down at once. Four philosophers share five forks. Even if each seated one holds a fork, one fork is still free, and the seated philosopher next to it can pick it up and eat. A Semaphore(n - 1) from Synchronizers is the waiter, one chair short:

Java
Semaphore seats = new Semaphore(forks.length - 1);   // the waiter: one chair short

seats.acquire();
try {
    eatWithBothForks();
} finally {
    seats.release();
}
Kotlin
val seats = Semaphore(forks.size - 1)                // the waiter: one chair short

seats.acquire()
try {
    eatWithBothForks()
} finally {
    seats.release()
}

Both fixes served all 1,000 meals in the Try it, in about 1.2 seconds, with no deadlock. A third fix, tryLock on the second fork with a random back-off, removes no preemption, but it brings back the livelock risk of the two polite diners in Deadlock, livelock and starvation. Use ordering when you can number your resources. Use the waiter when you can't, or when you want to cap how many threads compete at all.

Any number of locks can freeze in a circle. Take them in one global order.

A table of philosophers needs every lock to itself. The last problem is gentler, because most of its threads are happy to share.

sim.title: Three philosophers, three forks, left fork first
sim.intro: Each philosopher takes the left fork, then the right one. First let them eat one at a time. Then reset and give each philosopher exactly one step before anyone takes a second.

goal.say: All three ate, one after another. Now reset and let each philosopher pick up a left fork first: every fork is held, every philosopher waits for the next one's fork, and the table freezes.

try.title: Freeze the table, then fix it two ways
steps: Read Philosophers. Five philosophers try to eat 200 meals each, pausing 1 ms between their two forks. After 3 seconds, the demo asks the JVM which threads are deadlocked.
Run it as it is. Then run it with -Pargs=ordered and with -Pargs=waiter.
Compare the meal counts, the times and the deadlock counts.

code.title: Philosophers.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock; /** * Five philosophers, five forks, 200 meals each. Run as is (left fork, then right), * with -Pargs=ordered (lower-numbered fork first) or -Pargs=waiter (at most 4 may sit down). */ public class Philosophers { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "naive"; int n = 5; ReentrantLock[] forks = new ReentrantLock[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) forks[i] = new ReentrantLock(); Semaphore seats = new Semaphore(n - 1); // the waiter: one chair short AtomicInteger meals = new AtomicInteger(); Thread[] ps = new Thread[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { int left = i, right = (i + 1) % n; int first = mode.equals("ordered") ? Math.min(left, right) : left; int second = mode.equals("ordered") ? Math.max(left, right) : right; ps[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { for (int m = 0; m < 200; m++) { if (mode.equals("waiter")) seats.acquire(); try { forks[first].lock(); try { Thread.sleep(1); // reach for the other fork forks[second].lock(); try { meals.incrementAndGet(); } finally { forks[second].unlock(); } } finally { forks[first].unlock(); } } finally { if (mode.equals("waiter")) seats.release(); } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }, "philosopher-" + i); ps[i].setDaemon(true); ps[i].start(); } long t0 = System.nanoTime(); long deadline = t0 + 3_000_000_000L; // 3 s for the whole table for (Thread p : ps) p.join(Math.max(1, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000)); long[] stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads(); System.out.printf("%s: %d of 1,000 meals in %d ms, deadlocked philosophers: %d%n", mode, meals.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, stuck == null ? 0 : stuck.length); } }

alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Five philosophers, five forks, 200 meals each. Run as is (left fork, then right), // with -Pargs=ordered (lower-numbered fork first) or -Pargs=waiter (at most 4 may sit down). fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "naive" val n = 5 val forks = Array(n) { ReentrantLock() } val seats = Semaphore(n - 1) // the waiter: one chair short val meals = AtomicInteger() val ps = List(n) { i -> val left = i val right = (i + 1) % n val first = if (mode == "ordered") minOf(left, right) else left val second = if (mode == "ordered") maxOf(left, right) else right thread(isDaemon = true, name = "philosopher-$i") { repeat(200) { if (mode == "waiter") seats.acquire() try { forks[first].withLock { Thread.sleep(1) // reach for the other fork forks[second].withLock { meals.incrementAndGet() } } } finally { if (mode == "waiter") seats.release() } } } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() val deadline = t0 + 3_000_000_000L // 3 s for the whole table ps.forEach { it.join(maxOf(1L, (deadline - System.nanoTime()) / 1_000_000)) } val stuck = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().findDeadlockedThreads() println("%s: %d of 1,000 meals in %d ms, deadlocked philosophers: %d" .format(mode, meals.get(), (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, stuck?.size ?: 0)) }

try.expect: As it is: no meals at all in runs here (a lucky run may get one) and deadlocked philosophers: 5, found by ThreadMXBean, the JDK's window onto the JVM's threads, because the forks are ReentrantLocks. Ordered and waiter: all 1,000 meals in about 1.2 seconds, and deadlocked philosophers: 0.

sections.h: Many readers, one writer: who waits at the price board
sections.html:
The last puzzle brings back the price board from Don't share, with one change: this time the shop updates its prices in place, so readers and the writer have to take turns. Many threads at the tills (the cash registers) read prices all day, and readers can share, because two readers never get in each other's way. Now and then the owner changes the prices, and the writer needs the board to itself, so that no reader sees half a change. That's the readers-writers problem. Its real question is what happens when both are waiting, and every answer makes somebody wait longer than they'd like.

Readers first lets a new reader in whenever no writer is inside. It looks generous. But with a steady stream of readers that overlap, the reader count never drops to zero, so the writer never gets in. That's starvation: the program makes progress, but one thread never does.

Writers first makes new readers wait as soon as a writer is waiting. The owner gets in quickly, but with a stream of writers, the readers starve instead.

Fair order serves threads in the order they arrived. Nobody starves, and throughput, the work done per second, drops, because readers that could have shared now wait behind a writer who came first.

Let's watch the first policy fail. The Try it has four readers, each holding the read side for 2 ms at a time, overlapping, for one and a half seconds. After 100 ms, the owner asks for the write side. A textbook readers-first lock, written with synchronized and wait(), let the owner in only when the readers stopped on their own:

readers-first lock:     writer waited 1379 ms
ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited 2 ms

The new prices waited in the owner's hand until the shop went quiet. The second line is Java's own ReentrantReadWriteLock from Explicit locks, a lock with a read side that many threads can hold together and a write side for one. In its default, non-fair mode it promises no order, but a thread asking for the read side waits if the thread at the head of the queue wants to write. In practice, that keeps a stream of new readers from starving a writer. Fair mode gives strict arrival order:

Java
new ReentrantReadWriteLock();        // non-fair: a new reader waits if a writer is next in line
new ReentrantReadWriteLock(true);    // fair: strict arrival order, less work done per second
Kotlin
ReentrantReadWriteLock()        // non-fair: a new reader waits if a writer is next in line
ReentrantReadWriteLock(true)    // fair: strict arrival order, less work done per second

A lock that lets new readers pass a waiting writer can starve the writer. Make them queue behind it.

Before you choose a policy, ask whether the readers need a lock at all. If the writer replaces the whole board, the snapshot from Don't share lets readers read an immutable map with no lock and no waiting, and the question of who starves goes away. Many databases, the programs that store data for other programs, do something similar, which they call multiversion reads: a reader sees a complete older version while a writer works on the new one.

That's also where this lesson's tools stop. A pill, a lock order and a read-write lock each solve one shape of problem. None of them tells you whether your version works on a busy day. For that you need a test that makes threads collide on purpose, and that's where the next lesson goes.

try.title: Starve a writer
steps: Read ReadersWriters. Four readers hold the read side for 2 ms at a time, overlapping, for 1.5 seconds. After 100 ms, one writer asks for the lock. The demo measures how long it waits, first with a hand-written readers-first lock, then with ReentrantReadWriteLock.

code.title: ReadersWriters.java
code.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12; import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock; /** * Four readers keep the shop's price table busy for 1.5 s, overlapping all the time. One writer wants in once. * How long does it wait with a hand-written readers-first lock, and with ReentrantReadWriteLock? */ public class ReadersWriters { interface RW { void readLock() throws InterruptedException; void readUnlock(); void writeLock() throws InterruptedException; void writeUnlock(); } /** The textbook readers-first lock: a reader may enter whenever no writer is INSIDE. */ static final class ReadersFirst implements RW { private int readers; private boolean writing; public synchronized void readLock() throws InterruptedException { while (writing) wait(); readers++; } public synchronized void readUnlock() { if (--readers == 0) notifyAll(); } public synchronized void writeLock() throws InterruptedException { while (writing || readers > 0) wait(); writing = true; } public synchronized void writeUnlock() { writing = false; notifyAll(); } } static final class Jdk implements RW { private final ReentrantReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock(); public void readLock() { rw.readLock().lock(); } public void readUnlock() { rw.readLock().unlock(); } public void writeLock() { rw.writeLock().lock(); } public void writeUnlock() { rw.writeLock().unlock(); } } static long writerWaitMs(RW lock) throws InterruptedException { long end = System.nanoTime() + 1_500_000_000L; Thread[] readers = new Thread[4]; for (int i = 0; i < readers.length; i++) { readers[i] = new Thread(() -> { try { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { lock.readLock(); try { Thread.sleep(2); } finally { lock.readUnlock(); } // a 2 ms read } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); readers[i].start(); Thread.sleep(1); // stagger them so they overlap } Thread.sleep(100); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); lock.writeLock(); // the owner wants to change the prices long waited = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; lock.writeUnlock(); for (Thread r : readers) r.join(); return waited; } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { System.out.println("readers-first lock: writer waited " + writerWaitMs(new ReadersFirst()) + " ms"); System.out.println("ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited " + writerWaitMs(new Jdk()) + " ms"); } }

alt.title: ReadersWriters.kt
alt.html: package workbench.concurrency.l12 import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock import java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantReadWriteLock import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.concurrent.withLock // Four readers keep the shop's price table busy for 1.5 s, overlapping all the time. One writer wants in once. // How long does it wait with a hand-written readers-first lock, and with ReentrantReadWriteLock? private interface RwLock { fun readLock(); fun readUnlock(); fun writeLock(); fun writeUnlock() } // The textbook readers-first lock: a reader may enter whenever no writer is INSIDE. private class ReadersFirst : RwLock { private val lock = ReentrantLock() private val changed = lock.newCondition() private var readers = 0 private var writing = false override fun readLock() { lock.withLock { while (writing) changed.await(); readers++ } } override fun readUnlock() { lock.withLock { if (--readers == 0) changed.signalAll() } } override fun writeLock() { lock.withLock { while (writing || readers > 0) changed.await(); writing = true } } override fun writeUnlock() { lock.withLock { writing = false; changed.signalAll() } } } private class Jdk : RwLock { private val rw = ReentrantReadWriteLock() override fun readLock() = rw.readLock().lock() override fun readUnlock() = rw.readLock().unlock() override fun writeLock() = rw.writeLock().lock() override fun writeUnlock() = rw.writeLock().unlock() } private fun writerWaitMs(lock: RwLock): Long { val end = System.nanoTime() + 1_500_000_000L val readers = List(4) { thread { while (System.nanoTime() < end) { lock.readLock() try { Thread.sleep(2) } finally { lock.readUnlock() } // a 2 ms read } }.also { Thread.sleep(1) } // stagger them so they overlap } Thread.sleep(100) val t0 = System.nanoTime() lock.writeLock() // the owner wants to change the prices val waited = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 lock.writeUnlock() readers.forEach { it.join() } return waited } fun main() { println("readers-first lock: writer waited ${writerWaitMs(ReadersFirst())} ms") println("ReentrantReadWriteLock: writer waited ${writerWaitMs(Jdk())} ms") }

try.expect: Readers-first: the writer waits about 1,400 ms (1,379 and 1,362 ms in runs here), until the readers stop on their own. ReentrantReadWriteLock: 0 to 2 ms, because new readers queue behind the waiting writer instead of passing it.

compare.title: Stopping consumers: pills in Java, a closed channel in Kotlin coroutines

java.title: Java, BlockingQueue
java.html: for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { cooks.add(start(() -> { while (true) { String ticket = rail.take(); if (ticket == PILL) return; // each cook needs its own pill cook(ticket); } })); } for (Thread w : waiters) w.join(); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) rail.put(PILL); // 4 cooks, 4 pills for (Thread c : cooks) c.join();

kotlin.title: Kotlin, kotlinx.coroutines Channel
kotlin.html: // a Channel can be closed, so there are no pills coroutineScope { val rail = Channel<String>(capacity = 8) val waiters = tables.map { table -> launch { for (t in table) rail.send(t) } } repeat(4) { launch { for (t in rail) cook(t) } } // each loop ends when the channel is closed AND empty waiters.joinAll() rail.close() // "no more tickets": cooks finish the rail, then stop }

compare.note: With threads and a BlockingQueue, Kotlin code looks just like the Java version: the queue has no idea of "closed", so you still need one pill per consumer, compared with ===. Java's queue does its job well, and the pill is a small, honest workaround for what it lacks. The real difference comes with coroutines, Kotlin's lightweight tasks that the coroutines track covers. A Channel is a queue for coroutines, and it can be closed: close() means no more items, and every for (t in rail) loop ends once the channel is closed and empty, however many consumers there are. That removes the whole family of pill-counting bugs. coroutineScope also waits for every coroutine it launched, so there is no join loop to forget.

worked.title: Close the kitchen without losing an order

steps.say: The kitchen's program has two waiter threads that take orders from the tables and four cook threads, with a bounded rail between them. At closing time, someone wrote this. What happens to the tickets still on the rail, and to the dish a cook is halfway through?
steps.code: // Naive: stop now, whatever is on the rail void closeKitchen() { for (Thread c : cooks) c.interrupt(); for (Thread w : waiters) w.interrupt(); }

alt.html: // Naive: stop now, whatever is on the rail fun closeKitchen() { cooks.forEach { it.interrupt() } waiters.forEach { it.interrupt() } }

steps.say: Interrupting a cook that waits in take() stops it at once, so every ticket still on the rail is dropped. A cook in the middle of a dish may stop halfway and leave it unfinished. And a waiter interrupted inside put loses the order it was holding. Nothing throws, and nothing tells the customers.
Here's the orderly version, with a label on each step. open is a volatile flag the waiters check before they take each new order.
steps.code: void closeKitchen() throws InterruptedException { open = false; // 1. waiters stop taking new orders for (Thread w : waiters) w.join(); // 2. wait until no waiter can put again for (int i = 0; i < cooks.size(); i++) { rail.put(PILL); // 3. one pill per cook, behind every real ticket } long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(30); for (Thread c : cooks) { c.join(Math.max(1, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(deadline - System.nanoTime()))); // 4. one deadline for all } for (Thread c : cooks) if (c.isAlive()) c.interrupt(); // 5. still busy: interrupt as a last resort }

alt.html: fun closeKitchen() { open = false // 1. waiters stop taking new orders waiters.forEach { it.join() } // 2. wait until no waiter can put again repeat(cooks.size) { rail.put(PILL) } // 3. one pill per cook, behind every real ticket val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(30) for (c in cooks) { c.join(maxOf(1L, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMillis(deadline - System.nanoTime()))) // 4. one deadline for all } cooks.filter { it.isAlive }.forEach { it.interrupt() } // 5. still busy: interrupt as a last resort }

steps.say: Before reading on, explain to yourself why step 2 must finish before step 3 starts. Answer: a pill put while a waiter is still working can land in front of that waiter's last tickets. A cook that takes the pill goes home. With every cook gone and the rail bounded, the waiter then waits in put forever, and the shutdown hangs in step 2. Joining the waiters first means every real ticket is already ahead of the pills.

Step 5 is the safety net. If the oven breaks, the cooks can't finish the rail before the deadline, and interrupting them is then the right call. The orders they didn't finish were never marked as served. A program that records each finished order, as the bank recorded each payment in Race conditions, knows exactly which ones to pick up when it starts again.

lab.title: A pipeline that stops cleanly, and a table that can't deadlock
steps: Meet the two classes. SettlementPipeline is this lesson's kitchen in general form: producer threads put records (plain strings) into one bounded queue, and consumer threads take them and call process on each. DiningTable is the philosophers' table: dine(seat, meals, eat) has the philosopher in seat take two forks and eat, meals times.
Run the tests. All six fail. The three pipeline tests hit UnsupportedOperationException. The three DiningTable tests time out after 15 seconds each: the philosophers deadlocked.

Part 1: write SettlementPipeline.run. Create an ArrayBlockingQueue of capacity and a unique pill (new String("PILL")). Start the consumers: each loops on take(), stops at the pill (compared with ==), and otherwise calls process and counts.
Start one producer thread per inner list. Join all producers, then put one pill per consumer, then join all consumers, then return the count.
Part 2: fix DiningTable.dine so every philosopher takes the lower-numbered fork first. Keep reachForTheOtherFork() between the two forks.
Run the tests until all six pass, then twice more.
hints: Count processed records with an AtomicInteger, because several consumers add to it at once.
The second pipeline test checks that process is never called after run returns. If it fails, you return before joining every consumer.

For the table, compute a = seat and b = (seat + 1) % seats, then lock forks[min(a, b)] before forks[max(a, b)]. Only the last philosopher's order actually changes, and that's enough to break the cycle.
lab.done: All six tests in ClassicProblemsTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A poison-pill shutdown from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. You're given producer and consumer threads that are created but not yet started, and their shared BlockingQueue<String>. Write the code that runs them to completion with poison pills, plus the consumer's loop. Then check: when are the pills put, how many, and how does a consumer recognize one?

answer.html: static final String PILL = new String("PILL"); // a unique object, compared by identity static void runPipeline(List<Thread> producers, List<Thread> consumers, BlockingQueue<String> queue) throws InterruptedException { for (Thread c : consumers) c.start(); for (Thread p : producers) p.start(); for (Thread p : producers) p.join(); // every item is in the queue for (Thread c : consumers) queue.put(PILL); // one pill each, behind the items for (Thread c : consumers) c.join(); } // each consumer's loop: // while (true) { String item = queue.take(); if (item == PILL) return; process(item); }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: val PILL = String(charArrayOf('P', 'I', 'L', 'L')) // a unique object, compared by identity fun runPipeline(producers: List<Thread>, consumers: List<Thread>, queue: BlockingQueue<String>) { consumers.forEach { it.start() } producers.forEach { it.start() } producers.forEach { it.join() } // every item is in the queue consumers.forEach { queue.put(PILL) } // one pill each, behind the items consumers.forEach { it.join() } } // each consumer's loop: // while (true) { val item = queue.take(); if (item === PILL) return; process(item) }

recap: Producer-consumer: a bounded BlockingQueue between two speeds. A full queue that makes put wait is backpressure.
Poison pills: put them only after every producer has finished, one per consumer, and compare them by identity.
Dining philosophers is a circular wait. Take resources in one global order, or let at most n - 1 threads compete with a semaphore.
Readers first starves writers, writers first starves readers, and fair order starves nobody but gets less done per second.
ReentrantReadWriteLock makes new readers wait behind a queued writer, and fair mode gives strict arrival order. If writers replace the whole thing, an immutable snapshot removes the problem.
The limit: these tools fix the shape of a problem. Only a test that makes threads collide shows that your version works.

explain.prompt: Explain to a friend how you'd close a kitchen with 2 waiter threads and 4 cook threads so that no order on the rail is lost and no thread is left waiting.
explain.answer: First stop the waiters from taking new orders and wait for them to finish, so every real ticket is already on the rail. Then put four poison pills, one per cook, behind those tickets. Each cook keeps taking tickets until it takes a pill, so the rail empties completely and each cook stops exactly once. The pill is a unique object compared with ==, so no real ticket can look like one. Finally, wait for the cooks with one overall deadline, and interrupt any that are still busy when it passes. Whatever they didn't finish was never marked as served, so it can be picked up again later.

deeper.html:
Poison pills are one of several ways to stop consumers. Thread pools use interruption: shutdownNow() interrupts every worker, and tasks are expected to stop when interrupted, as A thread's life described. A poll(timeout) loop that checks a volatile flag is simple, but it makes shutdown wait for up to one timeout, and every loop must check the flag. Kotlin channels and reactive streams have completion built in, which is why they need no pills.

The dining philosophers problem has more solutions than the two here. Chandy and Misra's solution passes "dirty" and "clean" forks between neighbours on request, which avoids both deadlock and starvation and works across machines, at the cost of messages. A plain tryLock with back-off works too, but it needs randomness to avoid livelock. All of them remove one of the four conditions from Deadlock, livelock and starvation.

Readers-writers shows up all over databases. Many of them use multiversion reads: a query reads each row as it was when the query started, so readers don't wait for writers and writers don't wait for readers. That is the immutable-snapshot idea from Don't share applied to storage, and it's why you rarely meet this problem in plain database queries. Writers still wait for other writers on the same rows.

If you want to see these problems under a real stress harness, the jcstress samples include Classic_01_DiningPhilosophers and Classic_02_ProducerConsumerProblem. The next lesson shows how to run jcstress and read its results.
